api:
The public API of OV.GlobeRender (js/gfx/globe_render.js) is unchanged:
- Constants: ZOOM_RADII, PAL.
- draw(ctx, G|null, view) → {ms, base, light}
- pick(view, px, py), project(view, lon, lat), objectAt(G, view, px, py), objectsAt(G, view, px, py), countryAt(view, px, py), screenPos(G, view, ref), radius(view), visible(view, lon, lat), radarCircles(G)
- rotateBy(view, dx, dy), zoomAt(view, zoom, px?, py?), rotateTo(view, lon, lat, ms?, zoom?), zoomTo(view, zoom, ms?, px?, py?), fling(view, vx, vy), stop(view), update(view, now?) → bool, busy(view) → bool, prewarm(), invalidate()
- The view fields are the same as before.

What changed in behaviour, inside the existing contract:
1. Any camera change draws the coarse "moving" frame. This covers drag, fling, rotateTo/zoomTo, zoomAt, a cx/cy change from the side panel, and resizes. The only exceptions are the first frame (and the first frame after invalidate()) and a return to the exact camera already in the fine cache; both go straight to the fine frame.
2. The fine frame is rebuilt once the camera has been still for 260 ms. That 260 ms is counted on view.time or on the wall clock, whichever gets there first. So a frozen view.time (static QA) still settles, and slow frames (> 260 ms apart) no longer force a fine rebuild in the middle of a gesture.
3. busy(view) stays true until that fine rebuild.
4. When the camera is paused mid-gesture (same camera and sun as the last coarse frame), the half-resolution globe is reused without sampling again.

The moving frame:
- Biomes and shading are sampled in a single pass of about 16k samples.
- With dpr ≥ 1.5, the globe (atmosphere ring from a cached sprite, disc, light, halo) is drawn into a canvas at dpr/2 that covers only the globe's bounding box. It is then scaled ×2 with nearest-neighbour, in one drawImage, over the full-resolution stars. Markers, labels and radars stay at full resolution.
- With dpr < 1.5 it draws straight to the screen and copies the cached background.
- Cheaper vector operations: the sun glint is drawn on the ocean before the land, so the evenodd ocean clip is not needed; the land uses only its own clip; strokes are drawn outside clips; the dark coast outline is an offset hairline.

The rest (fine) pipeline is unchanged in its operations. It now copies a background (stars plus atmosphere) cached per size, centre and radius, and skips samples beyond R + 3·step that can never be seen. prewarm() is unchanged (geometry plus 0.5° textures).
summary:
Rotating the globe is now about 2.6× cheaper in total and 2.5–3× faster in frames per second. The literal target of ≤ 8 ms median `draw()` time is not met, though: the moving `draw()` now takes 28–44 ms in this container. Rest frames are pixel-identical to before. All 573 Node tests pass under `--strict`.

**Where the time went (Chromium profile and per-step timing, 1440×900 @2×)**
- Most of each frame was software raster, not JS: about 130–180 ms of main-thread CPU per moving frame against 10–17 ms of script.
- The biggest costs were:
  - the atmosphere gradient ring (about 49 ms);
  - the two coast strokes drawn inside the disc clip (24–42 ms);
  - three full-resolution scaled image layers for ocean, land and shade (16–27 ms each);
  - the evenodd clip for the sun glint;
  - a full-screen copy of the stars;
  - in JS, about 5–10 ms per frame of biome and shade sampling.
- There was also a bug in deciding when the globe is moving. With frames more than 260 ms apart, every rotating frame rebuilt the full-quality image: about 160 ms median, at 4 fps. The first frame of every drag did the same, causing a hitch.

**What I changed**
- Any camera change now draws the cheap moving frame. The full-quality image is rebuilt once the globe has been still for 260 ms, counted on the view clock or real time, whichever comes first. The first frame stays full quality.
- Biomes and shading are sampled in one pass of about 16k samples.
- On screens with dpr ≥ 1.5, the moving globe is drawn at half resolution into a canvas the size of the globe. It is then scaled up 2× in one step over the stars, which stay sharp. The atmosphere ring comes from a cached sprite, which is scaled during zoom animations.
- Cheaper drawing while moving: the sun glint goes on the ocean before the land, strokes are drawn outside clips, and the dark coast outline is a thin offset line.
- If the camera pauses mid-gesture, the half-resolution globe is reused without sampling again.
- At rest, the background (stars plus atmosphere) is cached, and samples that can never be seen are skipped.
- **Tried and dropped:** cube-map textures and a fast `atan2` (no gain here), pattern fills (slower than clip plus `drawImage`), and smooth upscaling (3× the cost of nearest-neighbour).

**Before and after** (same browser and harness, original file vs new; machine load 3–7, never quiet):

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Main-thread CPU per moving frame | 130–178 ms | 50–66 ms |
| Frames per second while rotating | 4.7–6.4 | 13.2–17.8 |
| `draw()` median | 10–17 ms | 28–44 ms |
| `qa/geo_check.mjs`, real mouse drag in the game | 6.7–11 fps | 18.5 and 27.2 fps (36/36 checks) |
| Idle frame | 1.2 ms | 1.2–1.3 ms (unchanged) |

- **Why `draw()` went up:** this Chromium has no GPU, so the half-resolution canvas is rasterised synchronously inside `drawImage` and counts as JS time. With a GPU in Chrome, and in Safari's GPU process, that work happens off the main thread.
- **The alternative I rejected:** the same new code drawing straight to the screen at full resolution meets the target (6.9–8.4 ms median, p95 11.6–15.7 ms). But it costs 117–135 ms of main-thread CPU per frame, at only 7–8 fps. The script-only share of the shipped version is about 5–9 ms per frame under this load. I kept the half-resolution version because it is faster in total and because Safari rasterises canvas on the CPU.

**Quality checks**
- Rest frames in all 13 scenes match the original file exactly (zero differing pixels; only the test page's ms text overlay was masked out).
- `qa/globe_check.mjs` passes 31/31. It now adds three moving-frame screenshots, a check that the still image after a `rotateTo` equals opening directly at that camera, and main-thread CPU per frame in its performance report.
- Three new tests in `tools/tests/gfx_globe.test.js` cover the half-resolution path, the dpr 1 path, the real-clock settle with a frozen view time, reusing the cached image, and slow drags.
- Screenshots of moving frames, cropped at full size, show the half-resolution globe looks like a non-retina screen while moving: coastlines slightly stepped, coast outline slightly thinner, markers and labels sharp.
deviations: The literal target of moving `draw()` ≤ 8 ms median and ≤ 16 ms p95 is not met in this container: the half-resolution moving path measures 28–44 ms median. This Chromium rasterises in software, so the half-resolution canvas is drawn synchronously inside `drawImage` and counts as JS time. I chose this path because it cuts total main-thread CPU about 2.6× (130–178 → 50–66 ms per frame) and raises fps about 2.7× here. The same code drawing directly at full resolution does meet the target (6.9–8.4 ms median, p95 11.6–15.7 ms), but costs 117–135 ms of CPU per frame at 7–8 fps.

The moving frame is not pixel-identical to the rest frame, as the brief allowed. While moving: half resolution scaled 2× with nearest-neighbour, about 16k samples instead of about 108k, the dark coast outline as an offset hairline, and the sun glint drawn under the land instead of clipped by an evenodd ocean path. Rest frames are pixel-identical to the original renderer.

The rule for when the globe is moving changed: any camera change now draws the moving frame (previously the first change after a pause rebuilt the full-quality image), and settling counts on the wall clock as well as `view.time`. This removes the hitch at the start of each drag and the full-quality rebuilds during slow frames. `busy()` keeps the same meaning.
open_issues: Please confirm on a real MacBook Air in both Safari and Chrome: run `node ovni-1999/qa/globe_check.mjs`. It now prints `draw()` time, main-thread CPU per frame and fps for rotating at zoom 1, at night and at zoom 3. Expect 60 fps there: with a GPU in Chrome, and in Safari's GPU process, the half-resolution raster is not on the main thread, and the script part is about 5–9 ms here on a contended vCPU.

The `jsDrawMs` figure in `qa/geo_check.mjs` (30 `draw()` calls back to back) now includes the synchronous software raster of the half-resolution canvas, so it reads about 47 ms in this container. Read it alongside the drag fps in the same script, which went from 6.7–11 fps to 18.5–27 fps. `geo_check` passes 36/36; I only ran it, no change is needed in `geo_check` or `geo_ui.js`.

Unchanged from before: when the clock runs fast and the sun moves every frame, the light layer is rebuilt at full resolution (about 55 ms per draw here; `geo_ui` throttles these draws to 10 Hz). A possible follow-up is to apply the same half-resolution approach to the light layer while the sun is moving quickly.

Building the full-quality image 260 ms after the globe stops costs one heavier frame (about 100–150 ms here, probably 20–30 ms on a Mac) while the globe is already still. It could be split across two frames if that is ever noticeable.
No change to `index.html` or `geo_ui.js` is needed.
